content: We have docs#flip and docs#Function.swap and these seem to be entirely identical (save for the latter being dependently typed). Should one be deprecated for the other?
The latter also works with dot notation
@Eric Wieser It "works" with dot notation, but not in the way you would expect.
In that the effect is surprising, or the mechanism is?
The effect
Oh no, it fills in the type argument!

import Mathlib

example (a b : Nat) (c : Nat → Nat → Type)
    (f : (a : Nat) → (b : Nat) → c a b) : c b a :=
  c.swap f a b
Is this a quirk of Function. or does this happen with all dot notation?
I think all dot notation fills in the first argument with the right type, rather than the first explicit argument
I believe Kyle had an RFC for marking which argument should participate
My very first Lean RFC is about this too: lean4#1629

(The motivation for this "first argument, even if it's implicit" behavior is that it makes dot notation consistent when you are using it on a typeclass instance, where the typeclass appears as an instance implicit argument.)
"first explicit argument if there is one, followed by first implicit otherwise" would seemingly work for that case too
It's quite uncommon for a typeclass to appear in both positions

Here's my current RFC about it: lean4#6489

The first RFC suggests looking for a self parameter, and the new one suggests looking for a dotParam-annotated parameter.

Eric Wieser said:

"first explicit argument if there is one, followed by first implicit otherwise" would seemingly work for that case too

An annoying complication is that somehow we have to interleave finding CoeFun instances. I suppose for Function it would be fairly rare for there to be a CoeFun instance, and there's no confusion between trying for a CoeFun instance and making use of an implicit function-type argument.

For "there's only one way to do it" purposes, dotParam seems like the right choice to me.

However, I'm feeling tempted to let self be used for this too. The main argument against self is that it tempts people to use it rather than a more descriptive parameter name.

Anyway, regarding the original question, I believe there are a number of examples where there's the dependently-typed version and the simply-typed version, and you sort of need both since the former is more complicated to elaborate and might fail so you want the second, but also you do want the more complicated one since not everything is simply typed.
I guess we could try making the one in core dependently-typed and see what breaks?
I'm wondering if it's a good use of time though. Usually we don't use these functions for plain functions, and at least in core we don't tend to write in point-free style.
Haskell programmers learning Lean might gravite toward flip, and I'd hate to see dependent type issues making their programming style not work for them.

I'm wondering if it's a good use of time though.

Well, if it works everywhere then that's perhaps an argument for dropping it; and if it doesn't, it gives us something to put in the docstring of Function.swap explaining why it can't replace flip
I'm not proposing trying to fix all downstream breakages, only check if there are any!
I want to resurrect this thread.

I think there's a few issues here really. Firstly, flip is not reducible and doesn't have good simp/grind theorems so it causes more things to choke than you'd expect. Secondly, IMO Function.swap is mis-named: if you consider Equiv.swap, that does something totally different, and while Prod.swap is related to Function.swap it isn't the same.

There are also places in Mathlib where we use flip and places that we use swap. docs#List.zipWith_flip uses flip, and to be fair it is the non-dependent case. But then docs#Function.onFun_swap_comm - but this is ALSO the non-dependent case. We're totally inconsistent.

I think if we are going to have the dependent and the non-dependent cases, we should call one Function.dflip and one Function.flip. There's actually a stronger argument to use Function. in the non-dependent case because the dot notation actually works! I think them being semi-reducible but having a good simp/grind-tagged apply theorem is the way to go too.
or you could call 'em swap. IDK.

There's issue #36902 by @Miyahara Kō btw
Also as mentioned upthread, dot-notation for the dependent version is in-the-works (lean#13244, lean#1629)

I agree we should rename to Function.[d]flip or Function.[d]swap (and when dot-notation is fixed delete the non-dependent version and take its name), but note that docs#flip is in core while docs#Function.swap is in Mathlib.
So this needs a core RFC to namespace it and upstream the dependent version.

@Snir Broshi In my experience sometimes it's useful to have the non-dependent version (because typeclass inference can get stuck on the dependent one). I think my instinct is we should NOT call it swap.

That means the RFC in core would be:

  • Rename flip to Function.flip. Try making this dependent and see if anything breaks.
  • Add Function.dflip IF it is necessary - i.e. if making flip dependent breaks stuff.

Then in Mathlib:

  • Deprecate Function.swap and Function.swap₂.

I would actually go a little further - I would define Function.swap in core (or at the very least in Batteries, but Batteries doesn't really tend to define Function primitives) as
def Function.swap (a b x : α) [BEq α] : bif a == x then b else bif b == x then a else x.

This amounts to the same as Mathlib's Equiv.swapCore, but I think it is useful to have this as the function (along with the obvious theorems about them). Clearly this would make the deprecation story for Function.swap in mathlib slightly bumpy - so I'd get that done first, but that would ultimately be my aim.
i.e. swap = "exchange two elements of a type", flip = "exchange two arguments of a function".
This being said: consider Prod.swap. There is something slightly odd here because actually this is more like a flip based on the above.
